title: Uposatha
hookLine: on moon days lay people may keep eight precepts for a day and a night (AN 8.41)

cards: Go to a temple in Sri Lanka or Thailand on the night of a full moon and you may see something unusual. People dressed all in white, lay people, not monks, staying the whole day and into the night. They skip dinner.
They leave the jewelry and the perfume at home. Nobody's watching a game on their phone. They aren't trying to become monks.
For one day and one night, they're living a little closer to how monks live. It happens every week or so, following the moon.

teach.h: A MOON DAY, ABOUT ONCE A WEEK.
teach.b: Uposatha: the observance day, following the phases of the moon. The full moon, the new moon, and in many places the half moons in between, so it comes about once a week.

teach.h: EIGHT PRECEPTS FOR A DAY AND NIGHT.
teach.b: On uposatha days, lay people may take eight precepts instead of five. Precept three becomes complete celibacy for the day. Then three more are added.
Not eating after noon. No dancing, singing, music or shows, and no garlands, perfumes or makeup. And no high or luxurious beds: you sleep on something simple.

A discourse in the Numerical Discourses lays out these eight, with a beautiful framing. For each precept, the lay follower reflects: the arahants, the fully awakened ones, keep this as long as they live.
For this one night and day, I'll keep it too, following their example. So it isn't a penance. It's a rehearsal, a day of borrowing a freer life.

The Vinaya tells how the gatherings began. Other religious groups met on these moon days to teach, and people came to listen. King Bimbisara noticed, and suggested that the Buddha's followers gather too.

teach.h: A KING, MOON DAYS, THE MONKS GATHER.
teach.b: So the monks began meeting on moon days, and later in the same chapter they are told to recite their monastic rules together, as they still do every two weeks.
Lay people come to the temple, listen to teaching, sit, and keep their eight precepts.
A day kept apart: white clothes, an empty plate after noon, a plain mat, and the moon.

how: On uposatha days, Theravada lay Buddhists who keep the day go to the temple, often dressed in white, take the eight precepts, listen to teaching and meditate; monks gather every two weeks to recite their monastic rules.

o: a day when lay people become monks
a moon day for keeping extra precepts
a yearly festival for the Buddha's birth

games.q: match the piece of the uposatha day.
p: one of the three added precepts
the example lay people follow for a day
the king who suggested moon-day gatherings

s: on uposatha, lay people become monks for the day
they stay lay people; they keep eight precepts for one day and night.
the eight precepts include not eating after noon
along with celibacy for the day, no entertainment or adornment, and simple beds.
the moon-day gatherings began with a king's suggestion
the Vinaya says King Bimbisara proposed that the Buddha's followers gather on those days too.

games.q: you're keeping eight precepts for the day. it's 3 p.m. and a friend offers you a slice of cake. what does the uposatha day ask?
o: thank them and save it for tomorrow.
games.why: the sixth precept is not eating after noon. one way to keep the day is to save the gift for the next morning.

practice: Picture the temple courtyard on a full-moon night: white clothes, a quiet crowd, the moon coming up over the roof.

Then picture one day in your own life kept a little apart, and what you might set down for it: the evening snack, the music, the scrolling. Nothing to decide now; just feel what a simpler day might be like.

wordCard.voice: Uposatha. The observance day on the full moon, the new moon and the half moons, when lay people may keep eight precepts for a day and a night.

orig.note: Pali: the observance day, kept on the moon days.

carryVoice: Your line: a day kept apart. It isn't a penance; it's a rehearsal. See you tomorrow.
